items.title: John Altman interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 14, 2023
items.q: And they played “Shake, Rattle & Roll,” Franny Beecher was there, a great jazz guitarist, Joey Ambrose, the great jazz tenor player, Marshall Little, you know they were all swing musicians, western swing. And they swung like crazy. I mean I got to play on two or three numbers

ctx.x: I was going to say, that ages you. That’s fascinating stuff. Just a couple more things here. You had made a statement I believe you were taking about the song “Rock Around the Clock” that there was very little teenage music before that. I’m fascinated by that transition from what we’ll call swing into rock and it’s always struck me that “Rock Around the Clock” is actually a swing tune.

Oh totally. And I got to — which, I think I probably mentioned or you might know, when they had 50 years of “Blackboard Jungle” I got to play with the original Comets so it’s basically everybody who was on the original record apart from Bill Haley and my friend Billy Gusack who played drums because they reckoned that the drummer, Dick, sped up, so they wanted someone to keep the tempo. Anyway so it was basically the original band that toured with Bill Haley. And they played “Shake, Rattle & Roll,” Franny Beecher…

the Clock” and “Shake, Rattle & Roll” and all these things, were western swing. Absolutely. And the whole rhythmic feel was totally different to that sort of [scats] rock & roll thing that everybody thought straight eighths. It was swing. And it was so infectious, it was incredible. And you could say yeah, this is why they succeeded you know. It was in that tradition. It was swing.
